passage: In a kindergarten in Krakow, Mrs. Nowak rang the tidy-up bell. "Whoever tidies gets a sticker." Olga, five, raced around dropping blocks into the tub. Yosef stayed on the rug with his puzzle. "Why are you so fast?" he asked. "For the star sticker," Olga said. "And if you don't tidy, you can't go to the garden." Yosef glanced at the door, then shoved his puzzle into its box. When Mrs. Nowak turned away for a moment, Olga slid a block under the shelf instead of carrying it to the tub.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Nowak say whoever tidies would get?
qa.a: Whoever tidies gets a sticker.

qa.q: Why did Olga tidy so quickly?
qa.a: Olga was eager to win the star sticker and did not want to miss going to the garden.

qa.q: How could Mrs. Nowak help Olga think beyond the sticker?
qa.a: She could ask, "What happens to our room when blocks are left out?" and point out how tidying helps everyone find toys.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Nowak see the block under the shelf when she finds it?
qa.a: She may realise the children are tidying mainly to earn a sticker, and that the rule works only while she is watching.

grounding: It shows young children following a rule for a reward or to avoid losing garden time, and dropping it when unwatched.

passage: The primary-wing corridor was freshly mopped, and Sangeeta Ma'am stood at the far end. "Walk, children." Mehak, five, slowed to tiny steps, eyes fixed on Ma'am. "If we run, Principal Sir will shout," she told her friend. Halfway down, Sangeeta Ma'am turned to help a crying boy. Mehak broke into a run at once, skidded on the wet floor and grabbed the railing. When Ma'am looked back, Mehak was walking again, very slowly, hands folded in front of her.

qa.q: Why did Mehak say they should not run?
qa.a: Because Principal Sir will shout.

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to feel about the walking rule, given she ran the moment Ma'am turned away?
qa.a: She seems nervous of being scolded rather than convinced by the rule, so she walks slowly only while Ma'am is watching.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta Ma'am say to help Mehak understand the rule?
qa.a: She could point to the wet floor and say, "Walking keeps you from slipping," linking the rule to safety instead of fear.

qa.q: What would change if Mehak thought about her own skid on the wet floor?
qa.a: She might begin to see that the rule protects her, not only that breaking it brings a scolding.

grounding: It shows a five-year-old obeying a rule only to avoid punishment while an adult is watching.

passage: My name is Nikita, and I babysit Afreen in the evenings. She's five. Tonight I said, "Brush your teeth, please." She asked, "What will I get?" I said nothing, it's just bedtime. She sat on the floor. Then I remembered her Ammi's trick: "Two stories if you brush." Afreen jumped up and brushed so fast the foam hit the mirror. Afterwards she asked, "If I don't brush, will the tooth fairy get angry and take my teeth?" I think, for her, rules are about what she gets or what might happen to her.

qa.q: What did Nikita offer so that Afreen would brush?
qa.a: She offered two stories if Afreen brushed.

qa.q: How does Afreen seem to feel about brushing when she asks "What will I get?"
qa.a: She seems reluctant to brush, and her question shows she treats the rule as a trade for a reward.

qa.q: How could Nikita slowly add a better reason?
qa.a: Along with the stories, she could say brushing keeps teeth strong and let Afreen feel her clean teeth with her tongue.

qa.q: How does Nikita understand Afreen's way of thinking?
qa.a: She sees that for Afreen rules are about rewards or what might happen to her, not about the rule itself. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young child following a routine rule for a reward or out of fear of a consequence, seen by her babysitter.

passage:
Monday: Sarita told Eshaan, 'Tidy your blocks and you get a star sticker.' He tidied fast and stuck the star on his shirt.
Thursday: she asked again, with no sticker. Eshaan kept building. 'What will I get?'
Next week, she said, 'Blocks away, or no park.' He scrambled to fill the box, glancing at the door. 'Now can we go?' he asked, holding out his empty hands.

qa.q: What did Eshaan get on Monday for tidying?
qa.a: He got a star sticker, which he stuck on his shirt.

qa.q: How did Eshaan seem to feel about tidying on Thursday?
qa.a: He seemed unwilling, because there was no sticker; asking "What will I get?" shows he tidies mainly for a reward.

qa.q: What could Sarita do to help Eshaan understand why tidying matters?
qa.a: She could tidy with him and talk about how it helps everyone find toys, slowly adding reasons beyond stickers.

qa.q: What would change if Eshaan were a few years older?
qa.a: He might tidy because he understands it keeps the home nice for everyone, not only to get a sticker or avoid losing the park.

grounding: Illustrates a young child following rules mainly to earn rewards or avoid losing something, across days.

passage: The platform was packed, and the train was late. Ayesha gripped Mridul's hand. 'Hold on, or no chips.' He held tight, eyes on the chip packet in her bag. When a whistle blew and the crowd surged, she looked away for a second. Mridul let go to stare at a dog. Ayesha grabbed him back. 'Mridul!' He shrank. 'Are you going to scold me? I held most of the time!'

qa.q: What did Ayesha promise if Mridul held on?
qa.a: She said: hold on, or no chips.

qa.q: What was Mridul worried about when he shrank?
qa.a: He was worried about being scolded, which shows he follows the rule mainly to avoid trouble and get his treat.

qa.q: What could Ayesha say to help Mridul see why holding hands matters?
qa.a: She could explain calmly that crowds can separate them, so holding hands keeps him safe, not just earns chips.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel in that crowded moment?
qa.a: She probably felt a jolt of fear when he let go and relief when she grabbed him back.

grounding: Shows a young child obeying a rule for a reward or to avoid punishment, under crowded, time-pressed conditions.

passage: In their Delhi flat, Gurpreet, five, looked at the toys scattered across the floor. "If I tidy, do I get a sticker?" she asked her grandmother Nirmala. "Yes, one star." Gurpreet tidied fast. When Nirmala went to the kitchen, she stopped and sat down. When Nirmala came back, she jumped up and grabbed a car. "I'm still tidying! Can I have my star now?"

qa.q: What did Gurpreet ask for in return for tidying?
qa.a: A sticker, one star.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet jump up when Nirmala came back?
qa.a: She was worried she might not get the star if she was caught sitting down.

qa.q: How could Nirmala help Gurpreet tidy for reasons beyond the sticker?
qa.a: Talk about how nice the clear floor is, and slowly swap stars for thanks and a shared tidy-up time.

qa.q: What would change if there were no star at all?
qa.a: Gurpreet might tidy much less for now, since the reward is what drives her at this age.

grounding: Shows a young child following a rule mainly for an immediate reward and only while being watched.

passage:
"Lalit, stay in the shallow end," said Francis, the swimming coach. Lalit, five, bobbed in the water, his goggles pushed up.
"If I stay, do I get a lollipop?"
"We'll see. Why should you stay there?"
"Because you'll be cross."
"And?"
"And no lollipop."
"What about the deep water?"
Lalit thought hard. "It's too deep?"
"Right. It keeps you safe."
"Okay. But I still get a lollipop?"
Francis laughed. "Stay there all lesson and we'll see."

qa.q: Where did Francis tell Lalit to stay?
qa.a: In the shallow end.

qa.q: What does Lalit's question about the lollipop suggest about why he follows the rule?
qa.a: He mainly wants the reward and is worried about Francis being cross, rather than thinking about safety.

qa.q: What did Francis do to help Lalit think beyond rewards?
qa.a: Francis asked why the rule mattered, so Lalit could start linking it to safety.

qa.q: How might Francis see Lalit's answers?
qa.a: Francis likely finds them funny and normal for a five-year-old, and uses them to teach a little more.

grounding: Shows a young child following a rule for a reward or to avoid an adult being cross, and a coach nudging him towards safety.

passage:
Teacher's note from Anand, Monday
Tushar (5) walks nicely in the corridor when he sees me, but runs as soon as I turn away. Today he asked, "If I run, will I lose playtime?" When I said yes, he walked. When I asked why we walk, he said, "So you don't shout." I explained that someone could get hurt, and later I saw him slow down near the steps on his own. I'll keep praising him when he chooses to walk.

qa.q: What did Tushar ask Anand about running?
qa.a: He asked, "If I run, will I lose playtime?"

qa.q: What does Tushar's answer "So you don't shout" suggest?
qa.a: He follows the rule mostly because he's worried about being shouted at, not yet because of safety.

qa.q: Why is Anand's plan to praise Tushar a sensible next step?
qa.a: Praise rewards the choice he makes himself and helps it become a habit.

qa.q: How might the other children be affected by Tushar's running?
qa.a: They could get bumped or hurt, especially near the steps.

grounding: Shows a young child obeying a rule only to avoid losing playtime or being shouted at, noted by his teacher.

passage: Behind the school in Barmer stood the headman's guava tree, heavy with fruit. Kunal, five, walked under it slowly and kept his hands in his pockets. "Why don't you take one?" asked his cousin. "Manjula Aaji said if I don't touch the tree all week, she'll give me gud on Sunday," Kunal said. "And the headman shouts." He looked up at a yellow guava and swallowed. "A big piece of gud," he said again, to himself, and walked faster.

qa.q: What did Manjula Aaji promise Kunal?
qa.a: She said she would give him gud on Sunday if he didn't touch the tree all week.

qa.q: What is Kunal feeling as he looks up at the yellow guava and swallows?
qa.a: He is tempted by the fruit, but the thought of the reward and the headman shouting keeps him walking.

qa.q: How could Manjula Aaji help Kunal begin to think beyond the reward?
qa.a: She could ask him how the headman might feel if his guavas went missing, so he starts to think about other people too.

qa.q: How does Kunal's cousin see the tree?
qa.a: The cousin sees easy fruit and seems puzzled that Kunal won't take one.

grounding: A small boy leaves a tree's fruit alone only to earn jaggery and avoid being shouted at.

passage: December in Durban was hot, and the Christmas biscuits sat on the table under a cloth. "Aren't you having one?" Aiko asked. Lindiwe shook her head hard. "Mama said if I wait until after lunch, I get a star on my chart." "Is it naughty to take one?" Lindiwe thought. "It's naughty because then you don't get the star. And no cartoon after." She sat on her hands. "Five stars and I get the red bucket." Aiko nodded slowly and sat on her hands too.

qa.q: Where were the Christmas biscuits?
qa.a: On the table under a cloth.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling as she sat on her hands?
qa.a: She was tempted, but eager to earn the star and worried about losing her cartoon.

qa.q: How could Mama build on Lindiwe's waiting?
qa.a: Mama could praise the waiting and also talk about sharing the biscuits fairly, so the reason grows beyond stars.

qa.q: Why might Aiko have copied Lindiwe?
qa.a: Aiko seemed to accept Lindiwe's reasoning that taking a biscuit was bad because of the lost star.

grounding: A five-year-old explains that taking a biscuit is naughty because it costs her a star and a cartoon.

passage: The Eid holiday was coming, and Jatin Sir's kindergarten class lined up for the sweet sevaiyan a parent had sent. Zainab stood very straight at the back. The boy in front of her tried to push forward. "Don't!" Zainab hissed. "Jatin Sir said whoever stands nicely gets the star badge." "So?" "And pushers sit on the bench." The boy stepped back. When Jatin Sir walked past and pinned a badge on her kurta, Zainab glowed and touched it the whole time she ate.

qa.q: What did Jatin Sir pin on Zainab's kurta?
qa.a: A star badge.

qa.q: How can you tell Zainab felt proud of the badge?
qa.a: She glowed and kept touching it while she ate.

qa.q: How could Jatin Sir help the children see a reason beyond badges for waiting in line?
qa.a: He could ask them how it feels when someone pushes in front, so fairness also matters.

qa.q: What would change for the boy if there were no bench and no badge?
qa.a: He might have kept pushing, since Zainab's warning worked only by naming the reward and the punishment.

grounding: A kindergartner stands in line nicely for a badge and to avoid the bench.

passage:
I'm Rekha from the next flat. On Diwali I was helping Lavanya's mother arrange sweets, and Lavanya, five, kept looking at the big laddoo.

Her mother said, "No sweets before puja."

Lavanya sat on her hands. She said to me, "If I don't touch, Mummy will give me the big one." She didn't touch.

After puja, she ran straight to her mother for it. I don't know if she thought touching was wrong, or just wanted the laddoo.

qa.q: What did Lavanya say to Rekha?
qa.a: She said, "If I don't touch, Mummy will give me the big one."

qa.q: Why might Lavanya have followed the rule?
qa.a: Rekha thinks Lavanya mainly wanted the reward, the big laddoo, and was eager and hopeful about getting it.

qa.q: How could Lavanya's mother help her understand the rule beyond the reward?
qa.a: She could explain why they wait for puja, in simple words, alongside the treat.

qa.q: How does Rekha see Lavanya's choice?
qa.a: Rekha is unsure whether Lavanya thought touching was wrong or just wanted the laddoo.

grounding: A neighbour observes a child following a Diwali rule mainly to earn a promised sweet.

passage:
Monsoon week one: Pradeep gives Sarika, five, a sticker each night she brushes her teeth. She brushes fast, then asks, "Where's my sticker?"

Week three: she asks, "If I brush, what do I get?" Pradeep says, "Clean teeth." Sarika frowns and doesn't move.

Week five: Pradeep says, "No brushing, no story." Sarika runs to the sink at once.

qa.q: What did Pradeep give Sarika in week one?
qa.a: He gave her a sticker each night she brushed.

qa.q: Why did Sarika frown in week three?
qa.a: Sarika felt disappointed and unconvinced, because clean teeth didn't seem like a real reward.

qa.q: How could Pradeep help Sarika move beyond rewards?
qa.a: He could talk simply about why brushing matters while keeping the routine, so she learns the reason too.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Sarika asks what she will get?
qa.a: Pradeep might feel amused but a little frustrated that she only brushes for a reward.

grounding: Across monsoon weeks, a young child follows a rule mainly to earn rewards or avoid losing her story.

passage:
The Eid market in Old Delhi was packed, and it was starting to rain. Devika Khala held Sabina's hand tight.

"Don't let go, or no balloon," Khala said.

Sabina, five, held on so hard her fingers hurt. When a monkey jumped onto a stall, she wanted to run and look, but she didn't.

At the balloon stall, she held out her other hand. "I didn't let go. Balloon, please."

qa.q: What jumped onto a stall?
qa.a: A monkey jumped onto a stall.

qa.q: Why did Sabina hold on so tightly?
qa.a: Sabina was eager to get the balloon, and worried she would lose it if she let go.

qa.q: How could Devika Khala help Sabina understand why holding hands matters?
qa.a: She could explain that the crowd is big and she wants Sabina to stay safe, not just promise a balloon.

qa.q: How might Devika Khala feel when Sabina asked for the balloon?
qa.a: She was likely relieved and pleased that Sabina stayed close.

grounding: In a crowded, rainy Eid market, a young child follows a safety rule mainly to earn a promised balloon.

passage: It was wedding season in Delhi, and the hall was crowded and loud. Mummy knelt beside Abhinav. "If you stay in your chair during the pheras, you'll get ice cream after." Abhinav sat very straight. When his cousin Gautam ran past waving a balloon, Abhinav gripped the chair. "I can't. Ice cream," he whispered. Later, when Mummy went to get plates, Abhinav hopped off and chased Gautam round a pillar. Seeing her coming back, he raced to his seat. "I sat the whole time!"

qa.q: What did Mummy promise Abhinav?
qa.a: She said he'd get ice cream after if he stayed in his chair during the pheras.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav race back to his seat when Mummy returned?
qa.a: He was worried about losing the ice cream, so he wanted her to see him sitting.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Abhinav understand the rule beyond the reward?
qa.a: She could explain simply why sitting matters during the pheras, such as letting everyone see and hear, and praise him when he remembers without a treat.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel if she found out Abhinav ran off?
qa.a: Mummy might feel a little disappointed, seeing that the ice cream only kept him seated while she watched.

grounding: Illustrates a young child following a rule mainly to earn a treat, and only while he is being watched.
